_comment: A record of attempts to improve the lifecycle classifier, kept whether or not they worked. Written by hand rather than by the trainer because several of these need dependencies the deployed container does not carry (torch, cleanlab) and are therefore not reproducible in a normal training run. Every figure here came from a grouped-by-provider evaluation on the same 23,748 records, using the same protocol as the shipped numbers.
protocol: 4-fold grouped by data provider; every test record from a repair organisation absent from training

baseline.label: Random Forest on word features, as shipped

experiments.name: Multilingual sentence embeddings
experiments.what: Replace hand-written keyword rules with a multilingual encoder (multilingual-e5-small), so fault descriptions in German, Dutch, French and English land in the same space by meaning rather than by a vocabulary someone wrote out.
experiments.why: Clearly the better representation: +0.146 macro F1 over the fault lexicon at the same end-of-life recall, which dissolves the trade-off between the two entirely. It cannot be deployed here. PyTorch is 514 MB and the model weights 702 MB against a 512 MB container, so the encoder does not fit in the environment this product runs in. Reported as a result rather than quietly dropped.

experiments.name: Confident learning (label cleaning)
experiments.what: The labels are technician judgements, and end-of-life rates run from 1.3% to 43.1% across venues. Confident learning estimates which labels are probably wrong from out-of-sample probabilities, and those rows are dropped from training only.
experiments.why: Flagged 33.6% of training rows as probably mislabelled. Macro F1 rose 0.030 but end-of-life recall fell 0.108 -- the metric the product acts on. Reading the flagged rows explains it: a few are plainly wrong ("SSD installed." labelled End of life) but most are real, hard cases. Removing a third of the data takes signal out with the noise.

experiments.name: French repairability index
experiments.what: France requires manufacturers to publish a 1-10 repairability score. 865 devices across 118 brands, joined to this dataset on brand and covering 35% of rows, as a device-level prior the model would otherwise have to infer.
experiments.why: Within noise, and slightly worse on macro F1. A brand's average repairability does not predict what happened to one specific machine on one specific day.

experiments.name: Venue reweighting (GroupDRO-style)
experiments.what: Weight every repair venue equally regardless of how many records it logged, so no large organisation dominates the fit. The cheap version of the standard domain-generalisation approach.
experiments.why: Behaved exactly as the WILDS benchmark reports these methods behave on real distribution shifts. Macro F1 improved and fold variance dropped sharply, but end-of-life recall collapsed from 0.638 to 0.235. It bought stability by giving up the only output the product uses.

experiments.name: Isotonic calibration
experiments.what: The model's end-of-life risk is multiplied by 15 and subtracted from a device's score, so it has to be a real probability rather than a number that looks like one. Fitted inside each training fold only.
experiments.why: Does not change what the model ranks first -- it changes whether the number it reports is true. Calibration error fell from 0.1407 to 0.0250: the model had been saying 33% where the real rate was 19%, so every assessed device was losing about 1.8 points it had not earned.

also_checked: The full 305,649-row dataset contains the same eight organisations as the 24,648-row IT subset, so using more rows adds no groups. Eight is a structural ceiling, not a sampling choice.

Grouping by individual repair cafe (1,021 of them) scores HIGHER than grouping by organisation (8), because training still contains other cafes from the same organisation. The stricter split is the organisational one.
